mainText:
**The Romance of the Neon Sign Restaurant**
By Henry Begler

My friend and I are obsessed with what we call "neon sign restaurants." This term refers to any restaurant over fifty years old in the greater Los Angeles area where atmosphere and ambiance are paramount. These include enchilada-margarita Mexican restaurants and tiki bars in the Valley, red-sauce establishments on the Westside, and seafood shacks along Malibu's Pacific Coast Highway. Generally, these restaurants are windowless, filled with kitschy decor and signed celebrity photos, and evoke an idealized time and place that never truly existed, such as Old Mexico or Italy from Hollywood movies.

Among the contenders for the best neon sign restaurant in Los Angeles, my favorite is the Formosa Cafe in West Hollywood, a Chinese joint dating back to 1939. While the exterior appears modest, the interior is surprisingly expansive, featuring a diner-style front room, a back room with a massive bar salvaged from the 1937 film *The Good Earth*, two smoking patios, and even a genuine 1902 Red Line Trolley integrated into the building. The lighting is dramatically film-noir, and the walls are adorned with signed celebrity photos and old news clippings, marking booths with the names of former regulars like Frank Sinatra, John Wayne, and Marilyn Monroe.

The history of the Formosa is almost too perfect; it was opened by three mob-connected showmen, one of whom was later found shot dead in a nearby phone booth. Bugsy Siegel allegedly ran a bookmaking operation in the back, and ownership later passed to bookie Jimmy Bernstein, who brought prizefighters and jazz singers to the restaurant, which was open from 9 a.m. to 5 a.m. By the 1980s, the establishment had become grungier, with peeling paint and cheap drinks, yet its faded glamour attracted a new generation of Hollywood hopefuls.

In 2015, the Formosa underwent a poorly received renovation, turning it into a soulless gray space. Following public outcry, it closed in 2016. Fortunately, the 1933 Group, known for restoring historic establishments, revived it in 2019, thoughtfully restoring its charm and improving the food. When I first visited post-renovation, I felt as if all the magic and mystery of Los Angeles was encapsulated within this restaurant.

Walking a few blocks north of the Formosa, you can find faux-Spanish haciendas and whimsical cottages amid modern apartments, remnants of an era that emulated exaggerated film-set features. Today, many new LA apartments resemble uninspired five-over-one blocks, and restaurants have shifted to farm-fresh, small-plate concepts with airy interiors. While the food may be better, the atmosphere feels profoundly unromantic compared to the neon sign restaurants. The Formosa and its counterparts stand as reminders that our built environment can be a canvas for imagination, allowing patrons to step into a low-lit dream. After a couple of cocktails, it becomes a truly enchanting place.
